title: A Promise After the Fall
lead: Humanity falls, but God does not end the story. He announces rescue at once.
questions: Who do I have a settled opinion about that I have never tested in an actual conversation?
Where in my life am I staring at the one prohibition today and no longer seeing the whole “you may” that God has given me?
When did someone outside the church last tell me something personal about their life? And if it has been a long time, what might they have sensed from me?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: We begin forty days with the worst day in human history. If hope is going to be anything more than a good mood, it has to survive a day like this one.

God told the man, “You may eat freely from every tree of the garden.” Only one tree was off limits. The serpent asks, “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’” It wasn’t a lie. It was a caricature. The great “you may” disappears, and all that’s left is “you must not.” Suddenly God looks like someone stingy and controlling. Eve didn’t adopt a new religion. She adopted a suspicion: that God can’t be trusted. After all, the tree of life grew in that same garden with no prohibition and no limits. The crisis happened at the one forbidden tree.

Then evening came. In this scene the humans are described by a string of frantic verbs: they knew, they sewed, they heard, they hid. God is described by one verb: walking. At the usual hour, “in the breeze of the day.” The man had changed, not God. God came to His ordinary meeting with people who had just done something that could not be undone.

And He asked a question: “Where are you?” It is God’s first question in the whole Bible, and He isn’t asking for an address. This is how a parent calls when they can see exactly where the child is hiding and want the child to come out on their own. In fact, in this entire scene God doesn’t speak a single accusation. He asks questions. The accusations come only from human mouths: he points at her, she points at the serpent. God asks; people accuse. We often stand with the accusers: someone stopped coming, and we know why. Someone got divorced, and we know whose fault it was. But people don’t come out of the bushes when they hear a verdict. They come out when someone calls them by name.

And then, in the middle of the sentencing, before anyone has apologized, comes the promise: the woman’s offspring will crush the serpent’s head. It is the serpent that is cursed, not the man. The gospel doesn’t start in Matthew. It starts here. Finally, God makes garments of skin for the two of them with His own hands and clothes them. Their covering of leaves cost a little work and a few leaves. The covering from God cost a life. They left the garden dressed in God’s promise of rescue.

If this is what the first day after the disaster looks like, then there is no day in our lives, or in the lives of those around us, that lies beyond the reach of the question “Where are you?” And as we read this story, let’s remember where we stand in it: not beside the judge, but next to those two in the bushes, clothed by the same God.

We begin forty days with the day everything broke. That is not an accident. If hope is going to be anything more than a good mood, it has to survive an encounter with the worst day in human history. The third chapter of Genesis describes exactly that day. We know it as the story of how sin began. Today we will read it as the story of what God does after disaster has already struck.

sections.heading: The Question That Changed the Picture of God
paragraphs: It all starts with the serpent’s question, and it is worth reading slowly. God had said: you may eat from every tree in the garden, except one. The serpent asks, “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’” That isn’t a lie. It’s a caricature. The great “you may” disappears, only “you must not” remains, and suddenly God looks like someone stingy who guards what is His.

Eve didn’t adopt a new religion. She adopted a suspicion. The whole dispute in the garden is a dispute about God’s character, about whether He can be trusted. That dispute didn’t end in Eden. Each of us settles it again every time we ask, on a hard day, whether God really wants what is good for us.

It is worth remembering, too, that the tree of life grew in that garden with no prohibition at all. They were free to eat from it, and no one did. They reached for the one forbidden thing. That is how suspicion works: an enormous gift drops out of sight, and a single prohibition fills the whole field of vision.

sections.heading: Fig Leaves
paragraphs: Before God said a word, the humans had already gone to work. “They sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.” In the original, the verb “made” is one that until now had been used only of the Creator’s work. Now, for the first time, a human being makes something on his own, and it is an attempt to cover his own shame with his own hands. Humanity’s first religious reflex after the fall wasn’t prayer. It was an attempt to cover up its failures.

In the Old Testament, nakedness usually means more than having no clothes. To be naked is to be exposed, unprotected, defenseless against attack. Before they sinned, they were naked and unashamed because nothing yet threatened them. Since that evening, every human being has walked through the world without protection and knows it. All our zeal for explaining ourselves and covering up began there.

sections.heading: He Came at the Usual Hour
paragraphs: In this scene the humans are described by a whole string of verbs: their eyes were opened, they knew, they sewed, they made, they heard, they hid. Frantic activity; no one stands still. God is described by one verb: walking. At the usual hour, “in the breeze of the day.”

The man had changed, not God. God came to the meeting at the usual time, to people who had just done something that could not be undone. The name “the LORD God” returns in the story at the very moment these two are hiding in the bushes. They are hiding from the One they were used to walking with.

This is the chapter’s first piece of good news, and it doesn’t yet need any promise: God does not stop coming because people have done wrong. That is exactly the kind of day described here. People who leave the church rarely leave over doctrine. Far more often they leave because they have concluded that after what they did, there is no way back. Someone has suggested to them that God no longer comes at the usual hour. Sometimes that someone was us. Not with a word, but with a look.

sections.heading: Where Are You?
paragraphs: This is the first question God asks a human being in the whole Bible, and He isn’t asking for an address. The Hebrew word that opens the scene is “called out.” It is a word for making contact, not for breaking it off. This is how a parent calls when they can see perfectly well where the child is hiding and want the child to come out on their own. God’s first concern after the fall was not to establish who was guilty but to win back the relationship.

In the scene we like to call the first trial in history, God does not speak a single accusation. He asks questions: Where are you? Who told you that you were naked? What is this you have done? There are accusations in this scene, but all of them come from human mouths. The man points at his wife, and in passing at God, who gave her to him. The woman points at the serpent. Within a few sentences the world’s first family turns into a courtroom where everyone is a prosecutor and no one accuses himself. God asks. People accuse.

There is more of that evening in us than we would like to admit. Someone stopped coming to church, and we know why. Someone got divorced, and we know whose fault it was. Someone came back after a year, and we know how long it will last. We have a complete set of conclusions about a person none of us has talked to in months. The greatest favor we can do one another over these forty days is to trade one ready-made conclusion for one real question. Like the one in the garden: Where are you? How are you really doing? People don’t come out of the bushes when they hear a verdict. They come out when someone calls them by name.

sections.heading: Knowledge That Did Not Heal
paragraphs: The serpent promised: your eyes will be opened, you will be like God, knowing good and evil. History’s first temptation wasn’t about pleasure or power. It was about religious knowledge: what is good and what is evil. And though that desire may have seemed reasonable, once it took the place of relationship and trust, it brought the fall. Look at what they did with their enlightenment: they noticed themselves, then their shame, and right after that the other person’s guilt. Knowledge of good and evil, cut off from their bond with God, instantly became a tool for judging.

Knowing the Scriptures is a gift, and no one here is urging you to set it aside. But it comes with a temptation older than every heresy: to know about instead of knowing, to be right instead of being close, to treat knowledge as proof that you stand on the right side. In the Bible, being chosen never meant being better. It meant having something to carry to someone. Abraham was chosen so that all the nations would be blessed through him, not so that he would have something to set him apart from the neighbors.

A simple test: when did someone outside the church last tell you something personal about their life? If it has been a long time, it isn’t necessarily because people are closed. Sometimes it’s because they sensed judgment before they had a chance to say anything.

sections.heading: Broken in Four Places
paragraphs: The effects of that evening reached further than we usually say. One crack split four relationships at once: humanity hid from God, the man and the woman stood facing each other instead of side by side, the ground began to resist, and creation became dangerous. Sin is never a private matter, because it strikes at relationships immediately. That is why the repair isn’t private either: when God lifts a person up, He also rebuilds in them the ability to be with others.

sections.heading: A Sentence That Was Not a Punishment
paragraphs: And then, in the middle of the sentencing, come the words on which the whole rest of the Bible stands: “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.”

Three things are worth seeing here. First, the curse falls on the serpent, not on the man. The man heard that his life would be hard and that the ground would bear the consequences of what he had done, but the curse itself falls on the serpent. Second, God is the one speaking: I will put. Enmity toward evil is not a natural reflex of fallen humanity. It is a gift. If God had not put it there, the human race would have remained on friendly terms with the very thing that destroyed it. This is a sentence of grace, not of punishment. Third, the proportions: the serpent reaches the heel, the woman’s offspring reaches the head. A bite on the heel hurts and can kill, but a crushed head ends the matter. No draw was ever in the plan.

No one has apologized yet. No one has shown remorse or promised to do better. The last thing God heard from these two was mutual blame. And that is exactly when the promise comes. The gospel doesn’t start in Matthew. It starts in the third chapter of the first book, on the darkest day in the garden, before anyone had a chance to repent.

sections.heading: Clothing That Cost a Life
paragraphs: The chapter ends with a gesture that is easy to read too quickly. “The LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.” It is the same verb as with the fig leaves: the humans made a covering for themselves, and then God made a covering for them. The whole difference lies in the price. One cost a few leaves; the other cost a life. In the ancient Near East, stripping someone of their robe meant taking away their standing, and putting it back on them restored their rights. God did more than cover their shame. He restored their dignity before He led them out of the garden. They left clothed by Him.

sections.heading: A Gate That Was Mercy
paragraphs: At the end comes exile and a guard at the entrance. It is hard to find good news in that, and yet it is there. The gate was closed so that humanity would not reach for the tree of life and be fixed forever in a state of separation from God. Had they eaten then, they would have lived forever, and forever cut off. The expulsion was an act of mercy, not of revenge.

And one more note that rounds this out. The cherubim who stood at the entrance to the garden to block the way reappear later above the lid of the ark of the covenant, in the place where, once a year, atonement was made for the sins of the whole people. The guardians of the prohibition later guard the place where sins are forgiven. And the promise later given to Israel says, “I will walk among you.” It is the same word used for God’s footsteps in the garden that evening. A story that begins with a closed gate ends, on the last pages of the Bible, with a sentence about God dwelling with people. Between the one and the other lies everything we will be reading about over the next forty days.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: God came at the usual hour to people who had just done the worst thing of their lives. He didn’t accuse; He asked. He gave a promise before anyone apologized. He clothed them before they left. If this is what the first day after the disaster looks like, then there is no day in our lives, or in the lives of the people around us, that lies beyond the reach of this question: “Where are you?” And as we read this story, let’s remember where we stand in it: not beside the judge, but next to those two in the bushes, clothed by the same God.
